In [[numerical analysis]], an [[iterative method]] is called '''locally convergent''' if the successive [[approximation]]s produced by the method are guaranteed to [[Limit of a sequence|converge]] to a solution when the initial approximation is already close enough to the solution. Iterative methods for [[nonlinear equation]]s and their systems, such as [[Newton's method]] are usually only locally convergent.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Gautschi |first=Walter |title=Numerical analysis |date=2012 |publisher=Springer / Birkhäuser |isbn=978-0-8176-8258-3 |edition=2nd |location=New York |pages=275 |language=en}}</ref>

An iterative method that converges for an arbitrary initial approximation is called '''globally convergent'''. Iterative methods for systems of [[linear equations]] are usually globally convergent.<ref name=":0" />
